witnesses.evidence_phrase: The first commandment teaches us that there is but one God, and that we ought to worship him only.
witnesses.rationale: Josephus paraphrases the first commandment as teaching that there is but one God who alone is to be worshipped, an exclusivity formula that runs alongside the Deutero-Isaiah no-other-god pattern the lexical verdict reads. This is an independent first-century Jewish witness to strict monotheism, the same one-God position the question contrasts with a plurality of divine beings. It is parallel because Josephus preserves the tradition in his own stream rather than depending on the canonical anchors.

extant_witnesses: MSS per Niese (A, M, V, W)

witnesses.text: The first commandment teaches us that there is but one God, and that we ought to worship him only. The second commands us not to make the image of any living creature to worship it. The third, that we must not swear by God in a false matter. The fourth, that we must keep the seventh day, by resting from all sorts of work. The fifth, that we must honor our parents. The sixth that we must abstain from murder. The seventh that we must not commit adultery. The eighth, that we must not be guilty of theft. The ninth, that we must not bear false witness. The tenth, that we must not admit of the desire of any thing that is another's.

witnesses.evidence_phrase: for this entire agreement of ours in all our notions concerning God ... We have one sort of discourse concerning God, which is conformable to our law, and affirms that he sees all things
witnesses.rationale: Josephus claims a single, undivided Jewish doctrine of God, one sort of discourse concerning God conformable to the law, contrasting it with the contradictory god-talk of other nations. This testifies that first-century Judaism held a unified strict monotheism, the same one-and-only-true-God frame the question sets against a council of divine beings. It is parallel because it independently preserves the historic Jewish position rather than deriving from the scriptural anchors.

extant_witnesses: Codex Laurentianus 69.22 (Latin tradition supplements lost Greek)

witnesses.text: And this very thing it is that principally creates such a wonderful agreement of minds amongst us all; for this entire agreement of ours in all our notions concerning God, and our having no difference in our course of life and manners, procures among us the most excellent concord of these our manners that is any where among mankind; for no other people but the Jews have avoided all discourses about God that any way contradict one another, which yet are frequent among other nations; and this is true not only among ordinary persons, according as every one is affected, but some of the philosophers have been insolent enough to indulge such contradictions, while some of them have undertaken to use such words as entirely take away the nature of God, as others of them have taken away his providence over mankind. Nor can any one perceive amongst us any difference in the conduct of our lives, but all our works are common to us all. We have one sort of discourse concerning God, which is conformable to our law, and affirms that he sees all things; as also we have but one way of speaking concerning the conduct of our lives, that all other things ought to have piety for their end; and this any body may hear from our women, and servants themselves.

witnesses.evidence_phrase: There is one true God only: but they who are called Gods, by an abuse of language, are numerous; on which account the holy scripture on the present occasion indicates that it is the true God that is meant by the use of the article, the expression being, "I am the God (ho Theos);"
witnesses.rationale: Philo states plainly that there is one true God only, and explains that anyone else called god is so named only by an abuse of language, marking the article in ho Theos as the signal of the single true God. This is a first-century Alexandrian Jewish witness that there is exactly one true God and that lesser uses of the word do not multiply the category, the same exclusivity the question sets against multiple divine beings. It runs parallel to the lexical verdict's one-God formulas rather than depending on them.

extant_witnesses: Greek MSS of the Philonic corpus (Cohn-Wendland base)

witnesses.text: What then ought we to say? There is one true God only: but they who are called Gods, by an abuse of language, are numerous; on which account the holy scripture on the present occasion indicates that it is the true God that is meant by the use of the article, the expression being, "I am the God (ho Theos);" but when the word is used incorrectly, it is put without the article, the expression being, "He who was seen by thee in the place," not of the God (tou Theou), but simply "of God" (Theou);

witnesses.evidence_phrase: for he, being the only true living God, is also really the Creator of the world; since he brought things which had no existence into being; and he is also a king by nature, because no one can rule over beings that have been created more justly than he who created them.
witnesses.rationale: Philo identifies the one true living God as the Creator who brought into being things that had no existence, setting an absolute line between the uncreated Creator and everything created. This bears on the question's claim that God is unchangeably one and that the Son is uncreated rather than a created being, since it locates all created reality on one side and God alone on the other. It is parallel because it independently preserves the Creator-creature distinction the verdict reads in Hosea 11:9 and the creation anchors.

witnesses.evidence_phrase: כָּל מַה שֶּׁבָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעוֹלָמוֹ, לֹא בְרָאוֹ אֶלָּא לִכְבוֹדוֹ ... ה' יִמְלֹךְ לְעֹלָם וָעֶד.
witnesses.rationale: This mishnah teaches that everything the Holy One created in the world he created only for his glory and closes by citing that the LORD will reign forever and ever, placing all created things under the one Creator. It preserves the rabbinic strict monotheism in which there is one Creator whose glory is the end of creation, which runs alongside the question's one-and-only-God claim. It is parallel because it transmits the historic Jewish position in its own rabbinic stream rather than deriving from the canonical anchors.

summary: The extra-biblical Jewish record independently attests the strict monotheism the question contrasts with a plurality of divine beings, namely the claim that there is one and only one true God who alone created and rules everything. Josephus paraphrases the first commandment as teaching there is but one God whom we ought to worship only, and in Against Apion he claims that the Jews alone hold one undivided doctrine of God conformable to the law while other nations contradict one another about the divine. Philo states that there is one true God only and that anyone else called god is so named only by an abuse of language, and he identifies that one true living God as the Creator who brought into being things that had no existence, drawing an absolute line between the uncreated Creator and all created reality. The Mishnah in Pirkei Avot teaches that everything the Holy One created he created only for his glory, closing with the affirmation that the LORD will reign forever. These witnesses are recorded as parallel rather than corroborating because each preserves the historic Jewish position in its own stream, Josephus as historian, Philo as philosopher, and the rabbis in the Mishnah, rather than depending on the scriptural anchors. Together they show that strict one-God monotheism, with a hard Creator-creature line that leaves no room for humans becoming gods or for a created divine being alongside the one God, was the settled Jewish frame in the world around Scripture. No witness complicates or contradicts the lexical verdict.
